title: Prisons under pressure: drugs, purposeful activity, staff and the IPP backlog
label: 20 October 2026 · Work of HM Chief Inspector of Prisons
summary: Charlie Taylor, HM Chief Inspector of Prisons, told the Justice Committee that the prison system shows stronger leadership and security than a decade ago but is threatened by rising drug supply (including drones and phones), cuts to education and purposeful activity, fragile mental-health transfers, and chronic staff and procurement problems. He welcomed moves to end IPP sentences but warned releases and tagging programmes risk public safety unless case-by-case support, community services and better data are in place.

chapters.title: Overall picture since 2020
chapters.takeaway: Prisons show stronger leadership and fewer escapes, but the system is under strain from population pressures, drugs and reduced activity.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Charlie, you started in 2020. Is the Prison Service better or worse today?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: It's mixed. Early on, during covid, prisons worked well with inspectors. Leadership has improved and escapes are much rarer. But population pressures, drugs and people locked up too long are major harms.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: You mentioned drugs and people locked in cells—many prisoners are held 22+ hours a day. What's the impact?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Long lock-ups corrode mental health, increase boredom and drug use, and stop prisoners gaining skills to rebuild their lives. That raises the risk of reoffending and wastes large public spending.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any big improvements you would flag?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Yes—better governors and leadership in many jails, and some prisons run very well. But overall the system is fragile and needs different priorities.

chapters.title: Purposeful activity and work
chapters.takeaway: Cuts to prison education and workshops are weakening rehabilitation at a time when productive daily routines could cut re-offending.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said purposeful activity scores worst historically. Has it improved?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Not really. Some prisons improved, but since last October there have been big cuts to core education, redundancies among teaching staff, and fewer English and maths places.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: What needs to change to fix this?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Prisons need to be reoriented as places of purpose: proper teaching, full working days in suitable roles, and incentives so prisoners build work habits that help on release.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are there examples of good practice?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Yes. Ranby and Hatfield run near-normal working days and link prisoners to employers. Oakwood lets prisoners earn responsibility. Haverigg builds employer ties for people with difficult records.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If employers want prison workers, what blocks expansion of paid work?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Constraints include tightened rules on temporary release, rapid churn of prisoners in category C prisons, and difficulties matching employers to prisoners' home areas.

chapters.title: Drugs, violence and security
chapters.takeaway: Drug supply—drones, phones and organised crime—is a major driver of violence and instability; fixing it needs joined-up action and improved prison craft.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: Your 2025 drugs report warned prisons were unstable. How effective are current measures?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Not effective enough. We need to cut supply and demand. Supply-fighting has been slow—responses to drones and phones lack proper, coordinated work across agencies.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: What practical steps work in prisons?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Get basics right: targeted moves for key prisoners, good searching and scanning, CCTV and ANPR, tackle staff corruption, and run strong recovery wings and incentivised substance-free living units.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: Chelmsford cut positive drug tests to about 15%—how?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Focused wing management, assertive monitoring of known dealers, good search routines, and leadership. No magic bullet, but the craft and attention matter.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: Should we separate big organised players into different units?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: There's a case for it. The system already has close supervision for the extreme cases; creating separation for disruptive organised criminals could reduce harm.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does reducing drugs also need better treatment continuity on release?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Absolutely. Treatments like Buvidal work well but aren't always continued on release. Homelessness on release also pushes people back to drugs; the handover must be stronger.

chapters.title: Mental health, women and children
chapters.takeaway: Prisons struggle to treat serious mental illness, women's needs are often acute, and young offenders need more time out of cells and better behaviour management.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Are prisons equipped to manage people with serious mental illnesses?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Confidence is low. Transfers to hospital under the Mental Health Act are slow—sometimes averaging months when the target is 28 days—and prisons are not equipped to treat those who refuse medication.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: What about the women's estate—are their needs different?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Women in prison often have extreme vulnerability—mental illness, trauma, addiction and homelessness. Some would be better managed in the community, and short custodial sentences often do little to help.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Children get a statutory right to 15 hours’ education—many get less. Why?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Young offenders often spend 18–19 hours locked up because of safety and keep-apart lists, so education attendance falls. Parc shows it can be done: clear rules, strong staff, and boys out 10–11 hours a day with good teaching.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: PAVA issues in YOIs—should we rely on it?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: We should avoid situations that make PAVA necessary. Parc manages without it; high PAVA use often reflects poor staff training, chaotic wings or disproportional use against young Black men.

chapters.title: Staffing, procurement and capacity
chapters.takeaway: Governors are skilled but hamstrung by central recruitment, low local hiring control, restrictive procurement rules and staffing limits that threaten plans for 14,000 new places.

turns.speaker: Janet Daby
turns.text: How is staff morale and recruitment?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Morale varies with how well a prison runs. Recruitment is patchy: remote or wealthy areas struggle and central hiring removes governors' say over who they get.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: Why can't governors recruit locally and interview properly?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: They could and many want to, but central systems are set up to fill pipelines. Local recruitment costs more administratively, but governors say face-to-face interviews would yield better hires.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: You put Wandsworth into special measures. The MOJ put in £100m—are repairs being done efficiently?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Procurement is a huge frustration—slow, costly and risk-averse. Governors often can't spend small sums locally and get tied into long procurement chains that blow up costs and delays.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: The Government plans 14,000 new places by 2031—realistic?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Building cells is one thing; staffing them properly is another. Some areas already struggle to recruit. Opening places without staff risks empty blocks or unsafe regimes.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Should we build less and rehabilitate better?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: If we could cut re-offending by small percentages through better treatment, purposeful activity and housing on release, we would reduce pressure far more cheaply than building at scale.

chapters.title: Early release, tagging and IPP reform
chapters.takeaway: Early releases and tagging can help population pressures but risk public safety without better probation, data, housing and tailored plans; ending IPP is welcome but needs careful, case-based work.

turns.speaker: Sir Ashley Fox
turns.text: Has the early-release scheme eased pressure effectively?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Some easing was necessary, but sending extra prisoners into stretched probation, housing and health services raises risks of quick reoffending and recall if community support isn't scaled up.

turns.speaker: Sir Ashley Fox
turns.text: Tagging on release—practical or haphazard?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: It's early to judge. Tagging can help some offenders stay away from crime, but homeless or chaotic people won't be tagged successfully. We need data on pilots before a nationwide roll-out is judged.

turns.speaker: Dr Shastri-Hurst
turns.text: The PM asked to end IPP in this Parliament. What would you advise?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Ending IPP is morally right; the injustice must end. But many IPP prisoners remain risky. The reform needs case-by-case assessment, prison-based programmes (like Aylesbury's phoenix wing), and strong community monitoring on release.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Many recalled IPP prisoners can't access courses they need. How fix that?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: The system must reduce waiting lists and move prisoners into open conditions where appropriate so they can take required courses. Otherwise, they stay stuck and can't progress to parole.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If the Government fail to deliver IPP reforms within the Parliament, will problems persist?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Yes—leaving people in limbo for sentences designed to prevent future harm but then not delivering a clear end is an injustice and damages individuals and public confidence.

chapters.title: Final priorities and what Parliament should focus on
chapters.takeaway: Parliament should focus on recruitment, giving governors local flexibility, procurement reform, and practical support for drug treatment, mental health transfers and IPP transitions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What should your successor prioritise?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Drugs and drones; recruitment and retention; and freeing governors to lead rather than be buried in procurement or central admin. Strong local leadership makes the biggest difference.

turns.speaker: Janet Daby
turns.text: Any specific asks for this Committee?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Scrutinise recruitment pathways and training, push for sensible procurement that trusts governors with small spend, and press for better data on what happens to people after release—housing and employment matter most.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could fix one thing, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: If I could be fanciful: no drugs in prisons. Practically: stronger local leadership—give governors the tools and trust to run safe, purposeful prisons.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Charlie. Good luck with the handover.

turns.speaker: Charlie Taylor
turns.text: Thank you. It's been a privilege; the people running prisons are extremely dedicated and need a system that enables, not constrains, them.
